ch.h: Twelfth in 2004, fifth today: the boom that India Shining only promised.
ch.f: In 2004 a government campaigned on “India Shining” and lost. Twenty years later the economy it promised is real: twelfth in the world then, fifth now.

ch.h: A quarter of a billion people lifted above the extreme-poverty line.
ch.f: In 2011 a poverty line of ₹32 a day caused uproar in Parliament. Since then the number of Indians below the world’s extreme-poverty line has fallen by more than a quarter of a billion.

ch.h: Child deaths before five fell from one in thirteen to one in thirty-eight.
ch.f: In 2004 one Indian child in thirteen died before turning five. Today it is one in thirty-eight. No other number in two decades of growth measures as directly what a country has given its people.

ch.h: From one Indian in fifty online to seven in ten, on the world's cheapest data.
ch.f: In 2004 one Indian in fifty used the internet. Today seven in ten do, on phones, on data that costs less than a cup of tea per gigabyte.

ch.h: Reserves up fivefold, a top-five stock market and a landing near the Moon's south pole.
ch.f: In 2004 India held $132 billion in reserves and its stock market ranked sixteenth in the world. It now holds more than $700 billion, its market is among the five largest, and it has landed a craft near the Moon’s south pole.

ch.h: An ID, a bank account and instant payments for almost everyone.
ch.f: An ID number for almost every resident, a bank account for almost every adult, and a phone payment system that now carries half the world’s instant payments.

ch.h: Highways, rail electrification, airports and metros built at record pace.
ch.f: India built highways three times as fast, electrified almost its whole rail network, more than doubled its airports and quadrupled its metro lines in a decade.

ch.h: From 3 to 162 gigawatts of solar in twelve years.
ch.f: In March 2014 India had under 3 gigawatts of solar power, about the size of two large coal plants. By June 2026 it had 162 gigawatts and the third-largest renewable fleet on earth.

ch.h: Open defecation fell from six in ten Indians to fewer than one in fourteen.
ch.f: In 2004 six in ten Indians relieved themselves in the open. Twenty years and more than ten crore toilets later, fewer than one in fourteen do.

ch.h: Forty crore people without power in 2004; almost none today.
ch.f: In 2004 forty crore Indians lived without electricity, nearly a third of all the people on earth who did. Today almost everyone is connected, and village power runs most of the day.

ch.h: The 5th largest economy, yet 143rd of 191 in income per person.
ch.f: India has one of the five or six largest economies in the world. Its average citizen still earns less than the average person in three of every four countries.

ch.h: Record harvests and free grain, but one child in three is stunted.
ch.f: India grows record harvests and gives free grain to 81 crore people. One in three of its young children is still too short for their age, and more than half its women are anaemic.

ch.h: The economy grew fivefold; the share spent on health shrank.
ch.f: The economy grew fivefold; the share of it spent on health shrank. Indians live longer than in 2004, but less long than Bangladeshis, and still pay for much of their care from their own pockets.

ch.h: Nearly every child is in school; fewer than one in four can read.
ch.f: Nearly every Indian child now goes to school. Fewer than one in four Class 3 children in government schools can read a simple Class 2 story.

ch.h: India grew rich in services and skipped the factory floor.
ch.f: Most economies that grew rich moved millions of people from farms into factories. India grew without doing so: manufacturing is a smaller share of its economy than when the boom began.

ch.h: Phones and bank accounts reached women. Paid work did not.
ch.f: Bank accounts, phones and cash transfers reached India’s women. Paid work did not. A smaller share of women are in the labour force than in 2004, and only twenty countries have fewer.

ch.h: Faster highways, more deaths: about 485 a day in 2024.
ch.f: India built highways faster than almost any country, and road deaths rose with them. Around the world deaths fell after 2010; in India they reached a record in 2024, about 485 a day.

ch.h: A solar superpower breathing some of the dirtiest air on earth.
ch.f: India built solar power faster than almost any country, yet its air is among the dirtiest on earth. Only five countries recorded worse air in 2025, and most of the world’s most polluted cities are Indian.

ch.h: Toilets were built; the sewers and treatment plants behind them were not.
ch.f: India built toilets for hundreds of millions of people. Building the sewers and treatment plants behind them came far slower: most urban sewage still reaches rivers untreated, and the Yamuna leaves Delhi thousands of times dirtier than it enters.

ch.h: Targets declared met before independent surveys agreed.
ch.f: Villages declared open-defecation-free, every village electrified, three-quarters of waste processed. Again and again India announced a target met before independent measurement agreed, while the surveys that could check the claims ran late or went unpublished.

ch.t: How Inequality Is Upending Social Peace
ch.h: The top 1% hold a larger share of income than at any time in a century.
ch.f: On the best available estimates, the richest 1% of Indians now receive a larger share of national income than at any time in the past century, and hold two-fifths of its wealth. The strain shows less in riots than in who protests: landowning communities that once felt secure now march for job quotas.

ch.h: Growth reached states, castes, tribes and faiths at very different speeds.
ch.f: Growth has reached India’s states, castes, tribes and faiths at very different speeds. Where the gaps follow the lines of identity, the easiest politics is to mobilise those identities and hand out cash rather than close the gaps.

ch.h: Everyone pays GST on soap; only 2.8 crore pay income tax.
ch.f: Every Indian pays tax each time they buy soap, a phone recharge or a bus ticket. Only 2.8 crore pay any income tax at all. Companies now pay less income tax than individuals do, wealth and inheritance go untaxed, and economists disagree sharply on whether the GST falls harder on the poor or the rich.

ch.h: Digital transfers closed old leaks, but the corruption score has barely moved.
ch.f: India digitised payments and pushed benefits straight into bank accounts, cutting some of the oldest leaks in the state. Yet its score on the world’s main corruption index has barely moved in a decade, more firms report bribe demands than ten years ago, and four in ten Indians who used a public service paid a bribe.

ch.t: Counted Out: Disability Rights and Welfare
ch.h: An ambitious disability law, and most disabled Indians never even counted.
ch.f: India’s 2016 disability law is among the most ambitious in the world, with 21 recognised disabilities, job quotas and accessibility mandates. The record on the ground is thinner: most disabled Indians are never counted, fewer than a third held a disability certificate in 2018, one in four works, and the central pension has been ₹300 a month since 2012.

ch.h: Children who enter school but leave, or stay and learn little.
ch.f: India gets almost every child into primary school but loses many before the end of secondary school, and many who stay learn little. A quarter of rural teenagers cannot read a Class 2 text; more than half cannot do simple division. These are the workers of 2040.

ch.h: Fast growth, while the share of adults with a job fell.
ch.f: For fifteen years India’s economy grew fast while the share of adults with any job fell. Work has picked up since 2019, but most of it is self-employment and unpaid family help. Educated young Indians are the most likely to be unemployed, and real wages for salaried workers have stalled.

ch.t: Gig Workers and the Risk of Revolt
ch.h: A young, connected, underpaid workforce set to triple this decade.
ch.f: India’s gig workforce is set to triple this decade. Most of it is young, urban, connected and increasingly educated, working ten-hour days for take-home pay that often does not cover expenses, with no employer, no pension and an app that can switch them off. Those are the conditions in which protest spreads. Nationwide delivery strikes came at the end of 2025.

ch.t: Old Before Rich? Ageing and Viksit Bharat
ch.h: Ageing at $2,400 a head, where Japan and Korea were six times richer.
ch.f: India crossed the line demographers use for an ‘ageing society’ in 2024, with 7% of its people over 65, at an income of about $2,400 a head. Japan and South Korea crossed it at six to seven times that. Births are already below replacement. The window in which a young workforce can make India rich is open now, and it narrows within a generation.

ch.h: Water per person down two-thirds, aquifers emptying in the north-west.
ch.f: India’s renewable water per person has fallen by two-thirds since 1961 and now sits at the edge of scarcity. Nine of every ten litres drawn go to farms, much of it pumped from aquifers that are emptying in the north-west. Taps have reached most rural homes; safe, reliable water has not.

ch.t: Too Much Rice, Too Little Dal
ch.h: Surplus rice and wheat; imported dal and cooking oil.
ch.f: India grows record harvests of the two grains the state buys, rice and wheat, and stores more than twice what it needs. It imports a fifth of the pulses and three-fifths of the cooking oil its people eat. The mix is set by procurement and subsidies, and the north-west’s groundwater pays for it.

ch.h: All wastewater, from kitchens to factories, and how little of it is treated.
ch.f: Every kitchen, bathroom, toilet and factory in India discharges wastewater. Only a third of homes drain into a closed drain, most urban sewage never reaches a working treatment plant, and no one reports how much industrial effluent is safely treated. Less than a third of India’s domestic wastewater is treated safely, half the world average.

ch.h: Green cover rises on paper while satellites count lost forest.
ch.f: On paper India’s forests are growing: official surveys show green cover rising to a quarter of the country. Satellites tell a second story. India has lost 2.3 million hectares of tree cover since 2001, old natural forests in the north-east and central India are giving way to mines, roads and farms, and much of the ‘gain’ is plantations.

ch.t: Heat Falls Hardest on the Poor
ch.h: A hotter India costs the poorest the most work and income.
ch.f: India is about 0.9°C warmer than in 1901, and 2024 was its hottest year on record. Heat now costs the economy hundreds of billions of dollars a year in lost work, and the loss falls on farm labourers, builders and street vendors who cannot stop working or buy cooling. Rising temperatures widen the gap between those who can escape the heat and those who cannot.

ch.h: Equal economies in 1982; China three times larger by 2004.
ch.f: In 1982 India and China had economies of almost exactly the same size, about $200 billion each. Twenty-two years later China’s was nearly three times as large. The gap opened in schools, clinics and factories before it opened in GDP.

ch.h: India's fastest growth, and the gap with China still widened.
ch.f: India grew faster after 2004 than in any earlier period, and still fell further behind China. India’s economy today is about the size China’s was in 2007; its income per person is where China’s was in 2001. On poverty India closed most of the gap. On health, women’s work, factories and research it did not.

ch.t: India’s Bargaining Power on the Table
ch.h: Three companies are each now worth more than India's annual output.
ch.f: In 2004 India’s economy produced more each year than the world’s largest company was worth, twice over. Today three companies are each valued above India’s annual output, and the ten largest are worth more than six Indias. Size at the table has shifted, and India has learned what that costs.

ch.t: The Bill for India’s Hardest Problems
ch.h: Heat, crashes, dirty air and malnutrition, priced as a share of GDP.
ch.f: India’s hardest problems are not only social failures; they carry a price. Heat, road crashes, polluted air, poor nutrition and wasted harvests each cost between half a percent and five percent of GDP a year. Added up, with care for overlap, the bill runs to several times what India spends on public health.

ch.h: How much wellbeing each rupee of growth actually bought.
ch.f: India grew 5% a year per person for twenty years. Turned into wires, roads and school places, that growth bought more than in most countries at India’s income. Turned into nutrition, health and clean air, it bought less. The next decade’s test is the rate at which income becomes wellbeing.

ch.h: Close the gaps in nutrition, health and learning with steady money.
ch.f: India’s biggest conversion gaps are in its people: children who are too short and too thin, women who are anaemic, pupils who cannot read, a health system run on a shoestring. Closing them is mostly a matter of money spent steadily, and of measuring what children actually learn and eat.

ch.h: Labour-intensive work that farm workers and women can take.
ch.f: India’s growth came from services and capital, not from moving millions into factory jobs. The next decade needs work that farm labourers and women can take: labour-intensive manufacturing, built for export, in places where people already live.

ch.h: India can build; now it must run and maintain what it builds.
ch.f: India proved it can build: highways, solar parks, toilets. Road deaths, foul air and untreated sewage show it has not learned to run and maintain what it builds. That is the work of cities and the state machinery behind them, and India’s cities are run on about 1% of GDP.

ch.h: Count commutes, clean air and reading as often as GDP.
ch.f: GDP is published every quarter; how long a commute takes, whether the air is breathable, whether a child can read, is measured rarely or not at all. A country that wants growth to become wellbeing has to count wellbeing, on time, through bodies the government cannot overrule.
